We are going to explain why the Rust borrow checker rejects two mutable references to the same data.
 The key reason is to prevent data races and ensure memory safety without a garbage collector.

 In Rust, the borrow checker enforces the following rules at compile time:
 1. You can have either one mutable reference or any number of immutable references to a particular piece of data at a time.
 2. References must always be valid (i.e., they cannot outlive the data they refer to).

 The reason for rule 1 (specifically, not allowing two mutable references) is to prevent data races.

Heapsort has a time complexity of O(n log n) in all cases—best, average, and worst. This is because the algorithm consists of two main phases: building a max-heap from an unsorted array, which takes O(n) time, and repeatedly extracting the maximum element from the heap and restoring the heap property, which takes O(log n) per extraction for n elements.
